chapter: Third reel: musicians and George Girard
title: George Girard at the Famous Door
summary: He praises Girard's tone and showmanship, tells how Girard turned down a Las Vegas offer before cancer surgery, and recalls the long nights.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: What I like about Connie Jones is not only his marvelous playing, but like you just mentioned, he plays a lot of tunes, good old Dixieland tunes, that a lot of the other Dixieland bands don't play. Oh yeah. And that's what I enjoyed the year working with Sharky's Dixieland band, with the old Sharky's Kings of Dixieland. I enjoyed that year with Sharky because Sharky played a lot of good old Dixieland tunes that I had not played with any of the other groups. Even when I was with Al Hurd or the late George Arrod, who I have a world of respect for the late George Arrod. Oh yeah. I couldn't wait to get to work at night to play with George. He had so much front line personality and such good tone quality on that trumpet. He played like Ray Anthony, man. He had beautiful tone quality. And as I mentioned before, the late George Arrod could make the audience laugh, he could make them cry, he could make it so quiet in that famous store where you'd hear pin drop. And he would imitate Jimmy Durante, he would imitate Libby Rache, he would imitate Sam Butera. He would imitate anybody, and just have the audience in stitches. I tell you, he was really a marvelous musician. And we were really all sad when he passed away because Blaze D'Antoni, I don't know if you heard of Blaze D'Antoni, wanted George Arrod to go to Las Vegas. And he wanted George to go for three months. I was playing with the band then. And George says, well I don't want to leave Hip Ginley that long to go to Vegas because Hip has been too nice to me. Hip had the famous dope. And it was decided that there was to be no option because he didn't want to go there for three months with an option to stay longer. He didn't want to leave Hip any longer. And then George came down with a cancer surgery before he could ever get away from the famous dope. And it was a known fact that he had about a year to live. And we had all made excuses to George on the side that we couldn't go. We made some kind of excuse that we couldn't go to Vegas for this reason or that reason. Because if we would have gone to Vegas, the man would have killed himself in three months instead of a year. And I know the musicians in the band would verify that station. We all made excuses. Because we wanted to keep George as long as we could. Because that's how great a musician we thought he was. He was a great loss to the music world.
I remember when he had that examination and everything. It just sounded hopeless from what Johnny Wiggs told me. Johnny I think was the one who told me about it. It was a shock.

Because, you know, George was so full of life. Oh, he was tremendous. Tremendous. I couldn't wait to get to work at night. I was getting three hours sleep a night in those days. Because in those days we were at the night shift. We would work nine or three and we'd be alternating with the Dukes of Dixieland or some other group like that or with Santa or some group, I don't recall. But at nine or three I'd get home at 315 or 320 and I had to get up at six and go to work to get ready to go to work because I had to be at work at seven o'clock. And I did that for three years.
Did you get a nap in the afternoon?

Yeah, I'd take a nap in the afternoon when I got home for about an hour and a half before I went to work. But I couldn't get to work. I couldn't wait to get to work with Gerard. Yeah. I enjoyed it that much.
